what_its_for: Insulin human is used to control blood sugar (glucose) levels in people with diabetes. It helps your body use sugar from the food you eat for energy, and it keeps your blood sugar from getting too high. It is used for both Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes.
how_to_take: Insulin human is given as a shot (injection) under the skin (subcutaneous). Common injection sites include your belly (at least 2 inches from your belly button), the front of your thighs, your upper arms, or your buttocks. Rotate your injection sites each time to avoid skin problems. Never inject into a vein or muscle unless your doctor tells you to. Always check the insulin before using it — regular insulin (R) should look clear, and NPH insulin (N) should look cloudy or milky. Do not use it if it looks unusual, has clumps, or has changed color. Wash your hands before every injection. If using a vial and syringe, draw up the correct dose carefully. If using an insulin pen, prime the pen before each use as directed. Pinch the skin lightly, insert the needle at a 90-degree angle (or 45 degrees if you are very thin), inject slowly, hold for a few seconds, then remove the needle.
dosing: Your doctor will set your specific dose based on your blood sugar levels, diet, activity level, and other health factors. Do NOT change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor or diabetes care team. Regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) is usually taken 30 minutes before a meal. NPH insulin (Humulin N, Novolin N) is an intermediate-acting insulin usually taken once or twice a day. Premixed insulins (70/30) combine both types and are usually taken twice a day with meals. Always use the syringe or pen designed for your insulin concentration (usually U-100) to make sure your dose is correct.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, check your blood sugar right away. For mealtime (regular) insulin: if you have not eaten yet, take it as soon as you remember. If you have already finished eating, skip that dose and wait for your next scheduled dose — do not double up. For longer-acting insulin (NPH): take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed one. Never take two doses at the same time. When in doubt, call your doctor or diabetes nurse for guidance.
storage: Unopened (sealed) vials or pens: Store in the refrigerator between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze insulin — throw it away if it has been frozen. Keep away from direct heat and light. Once opened (in use): Most opened vials and pens can be kept at room temperature (below 77°F or 25°C) for up to 28 days (4 weeks). Check the package instructions for your specific brand because storage times can vary. Never store your insulin in a hot car, in direct sunlight, or near a window. Write the date on your vial or pen when you first open it so you know when to discard it.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol or limit it significantly, as alcohol can cause your blood sugar to drop dangerously low (hypoglycemia). Do not skip meals after taking insulin — this can cause low blood sugar. Avoid unusual or intense exercise without checking your blood sugar first, as activity can lower blood sugar quickly. Do not share needles, syringes, or insulin pens with anyone else — this can spread serious infections. Avoid extreme temperatures — do not leave insulin in a hot car or freezing cold. Do not mix different types of insulin in the same syringe unless your doctor specifically tells you to.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you have signs of LOW blood sugar (hypoglycemia): shaking, sweating, dizziness, confusion, fast heartbeat, blurred vision, or fainting. Treat mild low blood sugar immediately with 4 ounces of juice or regular soda, or glucose tablets. Call your doctor if you have signs of HIGH blood sugar (hyperglycemia): increased thirst, frequent urination, blurred vision, or feeling very tired. Also call your doctor if: you have nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain (signs of a possible serious condition called diabetic ketoacidosis), you notice redness, swelling, or a lump at your injection site that does not go away, you are sick with an illness or infection (your insulin needs may change), or your blood sugar readings are consistently outside your target range.
when_it_works: Regular insulin (R) starts working within 30 minutes of injection, reaches its peak effect in 2 to 3 hours, and lasts for about 8 hours. This is why you take it about 30 minutes before a meal. NPH insulin (N) starts working in 1 to 2 hours, peaks in 4 to 12 hours, and lasts up to 18 to 24 hours. Premixed 70/30 insulin acts as a combination of both. You may start to see better blood sugar control within a few days of starting insulin, but it may take several weeks for your doctor to fine-tune your dose to reach your blood sugar goals.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Insulin human is the preferred insulin for managing diabetes during pregnancy because it does not cross the placenta and has a long safety record. Your insulin needs will likely change throughout pregnancy — your doctor will monitor you closely. Children: Insulin human can be used in children with diabetes. Doses are carefully calculated based on weight and blood sugar levels. Elderly: Older adults may be more sensitive to low blood sugar (hypoglycemia) and may not always feel the warning signs. Blood sugar targets may be adjusted, and caregivers should be aware of hypoglycemia signs. Kidney or liver disease: These conditions can affect how your body processes insulin and can increase the risk of low blood sugar. Tell your doctor about any kidney or liver problems so your dose can be adjusted if needed.
